title: Planning
one_line_goal: Plan written, checked and approved by you; no app code yet
summary: Build the project's memory (the wiki) and a plan portal for you, before any Ferrum code. You walked through the portal, answered the first two rounds of questions, approved both rounds of pages and signed off planning on 11 Oct.

tasks.title: Save the starting documents
tasks.what: Saves your original brief and your scoping answers as two files that are never edited.
tasks.why: If your words were lost or reworded, later pages could slowly drift from what you asked for, and nobody could prove it.
tasks.how: Copy both texts word for word into the raw-sources folder, mark them unchangeable and record their fingerprints in the wiki check report.
tasks.chain: Your brief and scoping answers are the ground truth → store them word for word, never edited → every later page can cite them.
tasks.check: Both files exist, are marked unchangeable, and their fingerprints are recorded.

tasks.title: Write five research notes
tasks.what: Five research notes: the wiki method, Tauri and WebView2, how to measure fairly, the plan-app tools and related work.
tasks.why: Tools change quickly. A plan built on remembered facts could rely on a feature that no longer works, and you would only find out in the middle of building.
tasks.how: Read the sources, give every web address an access date and label each claim as checked or uncertain.
tasks.chain: Plans built from memory go stale → research the wiki method, Tauri and WebView2, measurement, the plan-app stack and related work, with dated sources → decisions rest on checked facts.
tasks.check: Five notes exist; every source has an access date and a checked or uncertain label.

tasks.title: Write the wiki rules and live status
tasks.what: The wiki rulebook, Claude's start-up instructions and a live status file.
tasks.why: Without shared rules, a new session would not know how pages must look or where work stopped, and could redo or break earlier work.
tasks.how: Write the rulebook with page shapes and a fingerprint method, a short instruction file that links to it, and a status file with fixed fields.
tasks.chain: Many sessions and helpers edit the wiki → one rulebook (page shapes, fingerprints) plus a live status file → any session can pick up where the last one stopped.
tasks.check: The fingerprint script runs on the rulebook; Claude's instructions link to it; the status file has its required fields.

tasks.title: Describe the architecture and its parts
tasks.what: Overview and architecture pages, with one page per planned part of the app and what it talks to.
tasks.why: Some parts handle untrusted web pages. If the lines between parts are not drawn first, later code could let a web page reach something it must never touch.
tasks.how: Write one page per part, list its connections, and mark every connection between parts of different trust as crossing a boundary.
tasks.chain: The app has many parts with different trust levels → one page per part, saying what it talks to → security boundaries are visible before any code.
tasks.check: Every planned part has exactly one page; every link that crosses a trust level is marked.

tasks.title: Write the decisions and the risk register
tasks.what: One page per design decision (19 at the time; more came later) and a register of risks.
tasks.why: Without written reasons, a good choice can be undone by accident months later, and a known risk can stay unnoticed until it costs time.
tasks.how: Each decision page follows one template: the situation, the options, the choice, its effects and how it will be proven. Each risk page names the phase that must test it.
tasks.chain: Choices and risks get forgotten → one page per decision (19 at the time; more were added later) and per risk, with likelihood, impact and response → we can always see why, and what could go wrong.
tasks.check: 19 decision pages at the time, each with all required sections (later decisions came after); every risk has likelihood, impact, response and an owning phase.

tasks.title: Write the research plan pages
tasks.what: The research plan: questions, predictions, experiments, metrics and test workloads.
tasks.why: Numbers measured without a question and a prediction written first are easy to bend after the fact, and readers of the paper could not trust them.
tasks.how: Write one page per question, prediction, experiment, metric and workload, and make each page list the pages it is connected to, in both directions.
tasks.chain: Ferrum is also a research project → questions, predictions, experiments, metrics and test workloads, linked to each other → nothing is measured without a reason.
tasks.check: Links agree in both directions; no page states a measured number.

tasks.title: Write phase pages, index and log
tasks.what: A page per phase from P0 to P8, quality and how-to pages, root summaries, the page index and the work log.
tasks.why: Without an index and a log, things get lost between sessions: a page nobody can find is never updated, and its old text keeps misleading.
tasks.how: Write each phase page from the agreed page shape, add every page to the index as it is written, and start the log with the first sessions' work.
tasks.chain: Work spans nine phases and many sessions → a page per phase, an index of every page and a running log → you and Claude can find anything.
tasks.check: The index lists every page once; log headings follow the agreed format.

tasks.title: Check the whole wiki
tasks.what: A full check of the whole wiki and a fingerprint list of all raw source files.
tasks.why: Hundreds of pages written in parallel contain broken links and gaps. Building on them would spread the mistakes into every later phase.
tasks.how: Run every rule that can be checked by hand or by a text search, write a report with each result, and record one fingerprint per raw file.
tasks.chain: Hundreds of linked pages drift → run every rule by hand or script and fingerprint the raw files → work starts from a clean, tamper-evident base.
tasks.check: The check report shows zero errors; every raw file has a recorded fingerprint.

tasks.title: Install Node and record versions
tasks.what: Node 24 installed, with the exact Node, npm and git versions recorded.
tasks.why: Without recorded versions, a build that works today could not be repeated later, and a wrong Node version would break the app in ways that are hard to trace.
tasks.how: Install Node with the Windows package tool and save the version output. Any Node version other than 24 means stop and ask you.
tasks.chain: The plan app needs Node 24 → install it and record exact versions → builds can be repeated.
tasks.check: Node, npm and git versions saved; Node's major version is 24.

tasks.title: Create the plan app skeleton
tasks.what: The empty plan app, created with exact tool versions, plus three small feasibility tests.
tasks.why: Loose version numbers let tools update themselves silently, so a build that worked yesterday can break today for no visible reason.
tasks.how: Create the Next.js app with the researched settings, pin every version exactly, then run install, type check, style check and build.
tasks.chain: Loose versions break things later → create the web app with exact versions and three small feasibility tests → a stable base for the rest.
tasks.check: Install shows no version conflicts; type check, style check and build succeed; the feasibility tests pass.

tasks.title: Teach the app to read the wiki
tasks.what: A reader inside the app that loads the wiki pages and checks each page's header against the rules.
tasks.why: A page with a broken header would otherwise be shown with wrong or missing facts, and you could approve something that is not what the wiki says.
tasks.how: A small module reads the wiki folder while the app runs, splits off each header and checks it; tests use sample good and bad pages.
tasks.chain: The app shows wiki pages → a reader that checks each page's header against the rules → bad pages are flagged, not shown wrongly.
tasks.check: Tests on sample pages pass; the real wiki loads with zero header errors.

tasks.title: Fingerprint pages exactly like the reference
tasks.what: Page fingerprints computed in the app exactly as the reference script computes them.
tasks.why: If the app and the script disagreed on a fingerprint, a page edited after your approval could still show as approved.
tasks.how: Write the same method in the app's language and compare its results with the reference script on shared test cases.
tasks.chain: Approvals are tied to page fingerprints → compute them in the app exactly like the reference script → a changed page can never keep an old approval.
tasks.check: The app and the reference script give identical fingerprints on every test case.

tasks.title: Build the app's views and wiki check
tasks.what: The app's views (dashboard, roadmap, architecture, decisions, risks, research links) and an automatic wiki check.
tasks.why: Raw files are hard to read and easy to misread. Without views you could not review the plan, and without the check, broken pages would go unnoticed.
tasks.how: Build one view per area (dashboard, roadmap, architecture, decisions, risks, research links) on top of the wiki reader, and turn the wiki rules into an automatic check.
tasks.chain: You need to see the plan, not raw files → dashboard, roadmap, architecture, decisions, risks and research views, plus an automatic wiki check → the plan is readable and checked.
tasks.check: Browser tests open every view on a production build with no errors.

tasks.title: Build the approvals store
tasks.what: A local-only store for approvals, with safe file writes.
tasks.why: A lost or wrongly recorded approval could let work start that you never agreed to, or block work you did agree to.
tasks.how: One local entry point that accepts requests from this computer only and writes the approvals file safely; unit tests cover every approval state.
tasks.chain: Approvals must not be lost or forged → a local-only store with safe writes, every approval state tested → no approval is silently wrong.
tasks.check: Tests cover every approval state; requests from other computers are refused.

tasks.title: Build the approval screens
tasks.what: Approve, change and reject buttons in the app, with a badge when an approved page has changed.
tasks.why: It gave you a way to approve pages inside the app. It was removed with the first version of the app; you now approve in Claude Code, in chat.
tasks.how: Built in the first version and removed with it. Its check now runs the unit tests of the approval states instead.
tasks.chain: Approvals were first planned inside the app → approve, change and reject buttons with an outdated-page badge → later replaced: you now approve in Claude Code.
tasks.check: Unit tests: when an approved page changes, its approval shows as 'Approved, page edited since'. The old screens and their browser test were removed with v1.

tasks.title: Run the full plan-app test gate
tasks.what: One full run of every plan-app check, with the output saved.
tasks.why: Pieces that pass alone can still fail together. Without one full run, a hidden clash could reach you in the portal.
tasks.how: Run style, type, unit and browser tests and the build in one command, then the wiki check, and save all outputs as evidence.
tasks.chain: Each piece passed on its own → run every check together and save the output → proof the whole app works.
tasks.check: All checks pass in one run with zero wiki errors; output saved.

tasks.title: Portal v2, then your review
tasks.what: The read-only portal in plain words, then your walkthrough and your approvals.
tasks.why: You found the first version too technical. Without plain words you cannot judge the plan, and approving what you cannot read means little.
tasks.how: Claude writes plain-language text from the wiki for the portal. You read it and answer in Claude Code; Claude records each approval and revises.
tasks.chain: You found v1 too technical → rebuild it as a read-only portal in plain words, fed by text Claude writes from the wiki → you review it and approve in Claude Code; Claude records each approval.
tasks.check: The portal check reports clean; your approvals for the P1 pages are recorded.

tasks.title: Close P0
tasks.what: The close of P0: your exit approval and the first local commit.
tasks.why: Moving straight on would start the real app before you have checked the plan. The pause keeps you in control of when building begins.
tasks.how: Mark the phase for review, record your exit approval and a gate log entry, commit locally (never push), then pause until your explicit go.
tasks.chain: All checks pass and the pages are approved → you approve the phase exit in Claude Code → Claude pauses; P1 starts only when you explicitly say go.
tasks.check: Exit approval recorded; a gate entry in the log; work committed locally; no P1 work before your go.

test_gate.explanation: Every later phase builds on this plan → the portal's style checks, tests and build pass in one run, with the output saved → you read the portal and approve in Claude Code → only then does P1 start.

rows.proves: The portal's code is clean and consistent.
Wiki reader, fingerprints and approval states behave as specified.
Every tab works on a production build, reachable from this computer only.
The app and the reference script compute identical fingerprints.
You read every tab and popup and said what is unclear, until it reads clearly.
You answered or deferred each open question.
